papers.title: Electromechanical Drivers of Diastolic Dysfunction During Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Progression
papers.abstract: Aims: Diastolic dysfunction in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy reflects changes in sarcomeric function, electrophysiology, ventricular structure, and myocardial mechanics. Their effects on filling remain difficult to determine clinically. We sought to dissect these effects in MYH7-related non-obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy progression. Methods and results: We developed a human biventricular electromechanical model linking electrophysiology and calcium handling to contraction, ventricular mechanics, haemodynamics, electrocardiography, and myocardial strain. Stage I represented MYH7 sarcomeric dysfunction before hypertrophy; Stage II added septal hypertrophy; Stage III added increased myocardial stiffness. Secondary ionic remodelling was examined at each stage and severity. Sarcomeric dysfunction alone generated a low-volume hypercontractile phenotype before overt hypertrophy. Septal hypertrophy further constrained chamber filling, whereas myocardial stiffening exacerbated diastolic dysfunction and regional mechanical heterogeneity. Secondary ionic remodelling produced marked repolarisation abnormalities but, importantly, also prolonged calcium-tension dynamics and impaired relaxation, reducing ventricular filling to an extent comparable with structural remodelling in some disease states. Increasing ionic-remodelling severity progressively amplified these effects. Despite preserved ejection fraction throughout progression, ventricular volumes decreased while global and regional myocardial deformation deteriorated. Conclusion: Diastolic dysfunction was evident before overt hypertrophy and worsened as structural, mechanical, and ionic abnormalities were added. Preserved ejection fraction did not reflect reduced ventricular filling or deterioration in myocardial strain. Regional mechanical measures may therefore reveal disease burden not captured by ejection fraction alone. By separating individual disease mechanisms, in silico modelling may help link measurable biomarkers to their underlying causes and support mechanism-based patient stratification.

papers.title: Normative Auditory Nerve Physiology Reveals Myelin-Associated Changes in Neural Aging
papers.abstract: Communication difficulties in older adults are only partially explained by elevated hearing thresholds, suggesting that age-related changes in auditory nerve function contribute to disability beyond conventional measures of hearing sensitivity. Myelin degeneration is increasingly recognized as a fundamental feature of neural aging, yet its contribution to auditory nerve dysfunction remains poorly understood because validated in vivo biomarkers are lacking. We developed a normative physiological phenotyping framework by modeling the relationship between auditory nerve response amplitude and neural synchrony in younger adults and quantifying deviations from this relationship in older adults. Unsupervised clustering identified two auditory nerve phenotypes characterized by neural synchrony that was either as expected-or-better or poorer-than-expected relative to response amplitude, independent of age and hearing thresholds. The poorer-than-expected phenotype exhibited lower fractional anisotropy and higher radial and mean diffusivity in the auditory nerve, consistent with reduced myelin integrity. Human temporal bone diffusion MRI demonstrated changes in the same imaging metrics that corresponded with histological evidence of myelin degeneration, providing converging anatomical support for the imaging findings. Finally, the relationship between hearing loss and self-reported hearing difficulties differed between physiological phenotypes, demonstrating that poorer-than-expected neural synchrony amplifies the functional consequences of hearing loss. Together, these findings establish a physiologically defined, histologically validated biomarker of auditory nerve aging, implicate myelin degeneration as a previously underrecognized contributor to age-related communication difficulties, and introduce a general framework for identifying biologically meaningful neural aging phenotypes in living humans. Significance StatementCurrent clinical hearing tests are only weakly associated with the communication difficulties experienced by many older adults because they primarily assess hearing thresholds and do not capture age-related changes in auditory nerve function. We identify a rapid, noninvasive electrophysiological measure of auditory nerve synchrony that is supported by converging evidence from diffusion MRI and human temporal bone histology, providing evidence that auditory nerve myelin degeneration contributes to age-related communication difficulties beyond what is explained by audiometric hearing thresholds. By linking electrophysiology, neuroimaging, human temporal bone histology, and patient-reported outcomes, this work establishes a practical framework for detecting biologically meaningful neural aging phenotypes in living humans and advances the development of clinically accessible biomarkers of auditory nerve health.

papers.title: Real-World Improvement in Motor Status Among Regular Users of a Home-Based Brain-Computer Interface After Stroke
papers.abstract: BackgroundUpper extremity impairment persists in many stroke survivors, and few treatments are effective for severe chronic deficits. Brain-computer interface (BCI) therapy, which pairs decoded motor-intention-associated electrophysiology with sensory feedback, has improved upper extremity impairment in randomized trials, including in patients with severe paresis. Whether these benefits translate to routine care has rarely been evaluated. This study examined upper extremity motor recovery through 1 year among patients prescribed at-home BCI therapy in clinical practice. MethodsThis retrospective observational study included adults who were prescribed the IpsiHand System, an electroencephalography-based BCI, through a commercial US home therapy program, had a baseline Upper Extremity Fugl-Meyer (UEFM) assessment, and averaged >1 session per week through their last assessment. Occupational therapists administered the UEFM by video every 4 weeks. The primary outcome was UEFM change from baseline to week 12. A mixed model for repeated measures estimated change through week 52, with multiple imputation sensitivity analyses for missing data. ResultsOf 452 patients included in analyses (mean time since stroke, 5.4{+/-}5.4 years), mean baseline UEFM was 20.1{+/-}14.6, with 333 patients (73.7%) having severe motor impairment (UEFM 0-28). At week 12, mean UEFM change was 4.3 points (95% CI, 3.7-4.9; P<0.001), and 31.7% achieved the minimal clinically important difference (MCID) of 5.25 points. Mean change reached the MCID at week 16 (5.6, 95% CI [4.8, 6.4]). Model-estimated change in UEFM continued to improve through 1 year, being 6.1 (95% CI, 5.5-6.8) at week 24 and 8.1 (95% CI, 6.8-9.4) at week 52. ConclusionsAmong regular users of at-home BCI therapy in routine care, most of whom had severe chronic impairment, UEFM scores improved by 12 weeks, reached MCID by 16 weeks, and continued to increase through 1 year. At-home BCI therapy merits evaluation in randomized trials with follow-up beyond 12 weeks.

papers.title: Integrating GWAS meta-analysis with human brain cell mapping implicates the amygdala and cortical inhibitory interneurons in tinnitus
papers.abstract: Purpose: Tinnitus is a common and heterogeneous condition whose genetic architecture remains poorly defined and whose definition varies across studies. We asked which common genetic variants are associated with tinnitus, to what extent genetic associations are shared across heterogeneous tinnitus definitions, and in which brain cell populations tinnitus heritability is concentrated. Methods: Genome-wide association meta-analysis of 19 independent population-based cohorts from Europe and the United States (hereby named EARGEN), comprising 961,085 adults of European ancestry (75,584 tinnitus cases and 885,501 controls). Tinnitus was defined by self-report in 17 cohorts and by diagnostic codes in two. Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) based heritability and genetic correlations were estimated by linkage disequilibrium score regression, genes were mapped by gene-based association together with positional and expression quantitative trait locus mapping. Heritability enrichment was tested by stratified linkage disequilibrium score regression across 31 brain cell superclusters derived from post-mortem human brain donors, and across the 461 cell clusters that compose them. Enrichment was tested for replication in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under a self-report definition (114,325 cases, 201,343 controls) and a diagnostic-code definition (77,601 cases, 310,953 controls). Results: Five independent loci reached genome-wide significance (p < 5 x 10-8) on chromosomes 2, 8, 12, 13 and 16, two of which (rs10877884 and rs2147632) have not been reported previously. SNP-based heritability was 0.0137 (SE = 0.0009) on the observed scale and 0.0535 (0.0036) on the liability scale. Genetic correlations were significant with hearing loss, anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, chronic pain, and four further psychiatric, sleep and vestibular traits. Three superclusters showed a suggestive enrichment in the midbrain-derived inhibitory neurons, amygdala excitatory neurons, and medial ganglionic eminence interneurons at a false discovery rate (FRD) of 0.067, the two latter of which reached significance in the Million Veteran Program (MVP) under the diagnostic-code definition (0.030 and 0.006). At cluster resolution, the amygdala excitatory cluster was found significant (z = 4.82, false discovery rate = 3.3 x 10-4), whereas none of the ascending auditory relay cluster were found enriched (z [≤] 1.71, false discovery rate [≥] 0.21). Conclusion: Tinnitus-associated common variation concentrates in limbic and cortical neuronal populations rather than in the ascending auditory pathway. The predisposition to tinnitus therefore appears to be central and largely non-auditory in origin. The small number of genome-wide significant associations obtained despite a large sample emphasizes the need for more detailed and standardized phenotyping focusing on the tinnitus disorder.

papers.title: Nationwide Functional Profiling Enables Clinical Reclassification of KCNH2 Variants in the French LQT2 Population
papers.abstract: Background: The increasing use of genetic testing has identified thousands of KCNH2 variants associated with long QT syndrome type 2 (LQT2), yet most remain variants of uncertain significance (VUS). Translating functional abnormalities into clinically actionable evidence remains a major challenge. We established a nationwide functional genomics strategy to systematically characterize KCNH2 variants identified in the French LQT2 population and improve their clinical interpretation. Methods: We characterized 303 KCNH2 variants, including 201 VUS, using standardized high-throughput automated patch-clamp electrophysiology and complementary membrane trafficking assays. Nine electrophysiological parameters were integrated using MeTAL to predict variant-specific repolarization phenotypes under homozygous and heterozygous conditions. Modeled QTc values were compared with patient electrocardiographic data and variant-specific penetrance estimates. Functional evidence was calibrated against established benign and pathogenic variants using ClinGen-recommended categorical OddsPath and continuous likelihood-ratio approaches. Results: Multidimensional functional profiling revealed abnormalities not captured by current amplitude alone, identifying additional variants with clinically relevant repolarization defects. Among variants assessed under heterozygous conditions, MeTAL predictions showed 82.9% concordance with patient QTc phenotypes for ACMG class 5 variants, with apparent discordances partly consistent with incomplete penetrance. Continuous likelihood-ratio calibration demonstrated strong discrimination between established benign and pathogenic variants (AUC=0.936) and provided graded functional evidence for 76.1% of VUS. Integration of calibrated functional evidence into the ACMG/AMP framework enabled reclassification of 64 of 201 VUS (31.8%), including 7 as pathogenic, 46 as likely pathogenic, and 11 as likely benign. Conclusions: This nationwide study establishes a scalable framework integrating high-throughput electrophysiology, computational modeling, and clinical phenotyping to translate complex KCNH2 channel dysfunction into clinically interpretable evidence. The resulting reclassification of nearly one-third of VUS, together with the open-access HAMMER database, provides a resource to improve molecular diagnosis and risk assessment in LQT2.

papers.title: Cross-cohort validation of EEG biomarkers using a pre-registered three-criterion framework: a demonstration in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.abstract: Background. Despite decades of EEG biomarker development for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), no candidate has progressed to clinical deployment, partly because cross-cohort validation is rare. We aimed to develop and demonstrate a pre-registered three-criterion screening framework to identify which candidate EEG features show the combined properties required for biomarker translation: cross-sectional discrimination, within-subject reliability, and cross-cohort effect consistency. Methods. We pre-registered a validation framework adapted from FDA-NIH BEST principles and applied it to 18 EEG features across three independent cohorts: EEGET-ALS (six ALS patients, 170 healthy controls; home recordings over 17 days), UCL/Penn State (eight ALS patients; clinic recordings over 1-2 months), and a healthy adult test-retest reference (60 participants, three sessions over one month). Features were required to meet three pre-registered criteria: (1) cross-sectional discrimination (Cohen's d > 0.5), (2) within-subject reliability (ICC(3,1) > 0.6 in both ALS cohorts independently), and (3) cross-cohort effect direction consistency. Cross-cohort permutation testing (1000 iterations) and subject-level bootstrap resampling (500 iterations) were applied to assess robustness. Results. Three features met all three pre-registered criteria: gamma power, theta power, and spectral entropy. Cross-cohort permutation testing showed that no permutation, out of 1000, produced any feature in the three-cohort reliability intersection (Monte Carlo p = 0.001). Bootstrap resampling indicated that the composition of the selected set was sensitive to sample composition (median count 1, 95% CI [0, 4]), with gamma power (67% inclusion), spectral entropy (43%), and theta power (32%) the most stable features at a relaxed reliability threshold (ICC > 0.5); at the primary pre-registered threshold (ICC > 0.6), the corresponding inclusion probabilities are lower (57%, 27%, and 19%, respectively). A principal methodological finding was that cross-cohort differences in feature reliability were large relative to the apparent disease-associated signal, most clearly demonstrated by relative beta power (ICC = 0.09 in a home-recorded cohort versus 0.93 in a clinic-recorded cohort); because recording protocol, hardware, setting, population, and preprocessing all differ jointly between cohorts in this dataset, this is evidence of cohort-associated variability that plausibly includes a protocol contribution, not a separately identified, isolated protocol effect. Conclusions. This study provides a pre-registered, multi-cohort EEG biomarker screening framework for ALS with explicit bootstrap-quantified uncertainty. Gamma power, spectral entropy, and theta power are identified as priority candidates for prospective validation. A recurring methodological observation is that protocol-related cohort differences appear to contribute more to cross-cohort variability than disease-related effects within this dataset; because protocol is confounded with cohort, equipment, and preprocessing, this pattern is descriptive rather than causal. The observation nonetheless has direct implications for the design of multi-site EEG biomarker studies in neural engineering.
